extracted.intended_audience: researchers, institutional public information officers (PIOs), and science communicators who write scientific press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for composing a scientific press release that communicates research findings to non-specialist audiences, suitable for institution or journal publicity offices. Focuses on length, structure (headline, lead, body), style, visuals, and ethics (avoid overhype, note limitations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Length
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal length 300–500 words; one page maximum; up to 800 words for complex stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the release concise: 300-500 words is ideal for most stories, one page maximum. For particularly complex findings, up to 800 words may be acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline
rubrics_metrics.description: Short and enticing headline in active voice that avoids scientific detail and jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the headline plain English (not jargon). Use active voice and focus on the big idea rather than technical specifics. Example BAD: "Microvesicle-derived microRNAs are important for intercellular signaling in tumorigenesis". Example GOOD: "Cancer cells communicate through a new molecular messenger".

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead Paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead of 3–4 sentences that answers who, what, when, and why; use active voice and avoid jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead should state who did the work (the authors), what the main finding is, when/where it was published (journal and date), and why it matters (relevance). Keep it to 3–4 sentences and in plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body Content
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextualize the finding and describe how it advances scientific knowledge without giving nitty-gritty experimental details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the background and significance, translate technical concepts into plain language, and focus on implications and advancement rather than step-by-step methods or dense protocol details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes from Researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a brief quotation from a researcher that is insightful and authentic, not promotional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes should add context or interpretation, reflect the researcher's voice, and avoid sounding like marketing copy. Keep them brief and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact Information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide corresponding author name, email, phone, and institution; include PIO contact as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure media can reach authors or institutional communications staff quickly by listing full contact details for at least the corresponding author and a public information officer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active voice throughout (explicitly recommended for headline and lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active constructions increase clarity and immediacy. Avoid passive phrasing that obscures actors or dampens impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain Language / Avoid Jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate technical terms and use plain language suitable for non-specialist audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume specialist knowledge; explain or replace technical terms with accessible alternatives. Headline and lead should especially avoid jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Relevant Data and Statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims with relevant data and statistics where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give key figures or quantitative context that help reporters and readers assess the magnitude or reliability of findings, without overwhelming with technical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: Objective, Not Promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an objective tone and avoid promotional language or hype.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for measured, evidence-based wording. Avoid exaggeration, superlatives, or marketing-sounding claims that overstate the findings' significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide compelling visuals (photographs, infographics, diagrams) that help explain complex concepts; visuals should be clearly labeled and high resolution with captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose images or diagrams that clarify the story; label elements clearly and include informative captions. High-resolution files facilitate media use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include Journal Citation with DOI
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the full journal citation and DOI for the published study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise bibliographic information (journal name, date, DOI) so journalists and readers can locate the original paper easily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss Implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the implications of the research — how the finding advances knowledge or might affect the field/real-world outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify why the finding matters beyond the immediate result, but avoid speculative leaps; connect the result to broader questions or potential applications when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note Study Scope and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge the study's scope and limitations within the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefly state the study boundaries (e.g., model systems, sample size, preliminary nature) so readers and reporters understand how generalizable the results are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Overhype
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overstate findings or imply conclusions beyond the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautious language for early-stage or correlative results; distinguish between observed results and broader claims or future potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Findings from Speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly separate what the study demonstrates from speculation or next-step hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label speculative ideas as such and avoid presenting hypotheses or future applications as established facts.
